This is the exact event-demand feed that vacation-rental dynamic-pricing engines (PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, Beyond Pricing all cite PredictHQ as a data partner) plug into to move nightly rates around demand shocks. No data files are committed; it is a live-API pull (free tier exists but usage-limited).
why_useful: Standard, well-documented client for pulling a global multi-category event calendar (concerts/conferences/sports) with impact/attendance scores by location -- the general-purpose tool for the whole 'events and shocks' gap (#11), not just World Cup. name: COVID19USFlows (GeoDS Lab, UW-Madison)
what_it_holds: Daily origin-destination population flow CSVs derived from SafeGraph mobile-location trajectories, at census-tract, county, and state scale for the entire US, Jan 2019 through at least Apr 2021 (pre-pandemic baseline included). Tract-level files split into 20 parts per date for size. Published alongside a Scientific Data (2020) paper; MIT licensed; includes Python download/merge utilities. Split across multiple linked GitHub repos due to size limits.
why_useful: A genuine SafeGraph-derived mobility flow dataset committed to GitHub (not just a licensed sample) with county- and state-level granularity and a 2019 pre-pandemic baseline year — directly useful for calibrating a travel-mobility-to-nights elasticity model, and for testing whether short-term-rental demand co-moves with general population flow shocks (hurricanes, events). Fills part of gap #5/#11 and is a concrete method template (SafeGraph flow construction) relevant to gap #17 (methods/nowcasting with mixed-frequency mobility data).

name: Hurricanes_and_Migration
what_it_holds: Complete county-to-county migration flow matrices built from IRS-SOI data, 1998-2015, as CSVs in outflows/ and inflows/ folders (yearly matrices e.g. 0101in.csv, plus aggregated outflow.csv/inflow.csv). Also ships hurricanes.json: US federal disaster assistance records 1990-2018 with affected county FIPS, costs, casualties, dates. Python scripts analyze migration response to Katrina and Sandy.
why_useful: Long, clean, ready-to-use IRS migration panel (1998-2015) at county level -- can be extended/joined with post-2015 IRS SOI vintages to build a second-home / relocation proxy for STR demand in destination counties (sunbelt/vacation-market in-migration), and the hurricane-shock design is a template for isolating migration-driven demand shifts.

themes: Population, migration and second-home data (IRS migration, Census CPS, USPS change of address, second-home counts, holiday-home shares Europe)

Longer span than the mathewhauer repo (through 2015) and pairs migration directly with hurricane/disaster shocks by county — directly useful for gap 11 (events/shocks, hurricanes) and for modeling population/second-home exposure to storm-affected STR markets (Florida, Gulf Coast, coastal Northeast).

name: blackmarbler
what_it_holds: R package (World Bank DIME) that automates downloading and processing NASA Black Marble (VIIRS-derived) daily/monthly/annual nighttime-lights composites from NASA LAADS DAAC and aggregating radiance to any user-defined WGS84 polygon. No committed raw data (requires free NASA bearer token); demonstrated with 2012-2022+ near-real-time data (daily lag ~1 week). Actively maintained World Bank org repo.
why_useful: Same use case as blackmarblepy for teams working in R; redundant capability, listed for completeness.

One-command, point-in-time-capable pull of nightlights for any Airbnb market polygon (city/region) as a tourism/economic-activity proxy at monthly or even daily granularity, addressing gap #5 (engagement/activity proxies) and the broader satellite-tourism-activity theme; because it hits NASA's archive directly it could be re-run vintage-by-vintage for point-in-time construction.

One-command way to get admin2-level nighttime-lights time series for any tourism market worldwide (LatAm/APAC gaps in current holdings) without touching Google Earth Engine directly; complements idea above as a more turnkey pull.

name: HotelRec
what_it_holds: ~50 million TripAdvisor hotel reviews (largest public hotel-review dataset per the authors, vs 0.9M in prior academic sets). Each review has hotel URL, reviewer username, date, overall rating, title, text, and sub-ratings (sleep quality, value, rooms, service, cleanliness, location). International coverage (sample shows Italian hotels; likely global given TripAdvisor's footprint). Actual data is not committed to the repo -- hosted on a SWITCHdrive link, restricted to academic research use only. Cites Antognini & Faltings, LREC 2020. Repo itself: 17 commits, README + download pointer.
why_useful: By far the largest and longest-running TripAdvisor review corpus found. A review-velocity / sub-rating time series built from this (filtered to years with real dates, cross-referenced to ABNB peer-set cities) could proxy hotel demand momentum and sentiment ahead of MAR/HLT RevPAR releases -- addresses gap #8 (hotel supply/demand) indirectly via review flow as a leading indicator, and gap #20 partially (party-size/length-of-stay not present but trip-type sub-ratings sometimes are). Academic-only license limits direct commercial reuse but fine for an internal model.

time_coverage: Reviews with dates as early as ~2010 in samples shown; full range not confirmed

TripAdvisor review-volume-and-rating time series across a huge global hotel panel is a competitor/adjacent-supply engagement proxy (gap #9, and loosely gap #5 engagement signals) analogous to how Inside Airbnb reviews are used as a stays-index kernel for ABNB nights; review dates could be aggregated into a monthly hotel-demand pulse by market if the gated download is obtained.

name: hospitality-alt-data-dashboard
what_it_holds: Streamlit research tool building a near-real-time US lodging-demand proxy for MAR/HLT/H between earnings prints, from entirely free/keyless public sources: TSA checkpoint throughput (2019+), Google Trends brand search (pytrends, 6 hotel brands), BLS employment/JOLTS/PPI for traveler accommodation, yfinance prices/earnings dates, plus one committed hand-keyed file `data/reported_revpar.csv` (quarterly RevPAR for MAR/HLT/H with source URLs — same underlying idea as our 'MAR/HLT RevPAR from releases' but committed as a clean CSV with source links). README states explicitly this is a RevPAR *proxy*, not real STR data ("True RevPAR is STR data (paid)"), substituting BLS accommodation employment/PPI as demand/rate proxies. Reports its own honest backtest: deseasonalized MoM r≈0.41 (p≈0.003) vs RevPAR, but a composite TSA+brand-search+JOLTS signal fails out of sample (r=-0.14 steady state, p≈0.09 on a trading overlay). 32 commits, CI runs daily to refresh data and publish outputs as GitHub Actions artifacts; no paid keys required (optional BLS_API_KEY for higher limits).
why_useful: Directly on gap #8 (hotel supply/demand STR/CoStar proxy) and gap #17 (nowcasting method transparency). Even though it is explicitly a proxy rather than licensed STR data, it is a working, keyless, one-command pull architecture (TSA+BLS+PPI+Trends+yfinance) we could fork or mine for the BLS accommodation-employment/PPI series we may not already be pulling, and its self-reported failure of the composite signal is a useful negative data point consistent with our own TSA/Trends null results.
size_hint: small hand-keyed CSV + gitignored cached pulls; 32 commits
last_activity: not confirmed in fetch (active enough to run daily CI as of check)
duplicate_of_holding: Overlaps our existing 'MAR/HLT RevPAR from releases' and our own tested-and-failed TSA-throughput / Google-Trends constructions — still worth flagging for the BLS PPI/accommodation-employment proxy angle we may not have tried, and as a second working example of the same null result on TSA/Trends.

Directly matches gap #8 (regional RevPAR, hotel demand) with an actual committed multi-year reported-RevPAR CSV plus a live, no-key pipeline (TSA/BLS/Trends/yfinance) for hotel-brand demand proxies that read through to STR competitive pricing pressure.

The PPI Traveler Accommodation series is a monthly hotel-room-rate price index (adjacent to CPI lodging, arguably a cleaner room-rate proxy since it is closer to producer pricing) with an automated pull method; the committed reported-RevPAR CSV (2019-2026) is independently useful for gap #8 (hotel supply/demand RevPAR) as a hand-collected, already-tabulated series saving re-transcription from 10-Qs.

name: jtilly/cbpR
what_it_holds: R package that downloads and assembles panel datasets from the U.S. Census Bureau's County Business Patterns (CBP) program, aggregable to county/metro/micro level; `getFirmCount()`-style functions accept a NAICS code (demonstrated with a 6-digit code, so NAICS 721 'Accommodation' / 721110 'Hotels and Motels' is selectable), and years are user-specified (demo shown for 2000-2009, but CBP itself runs 1986-2023 annual).
why_useful: CBP publishes annual county-level establishment counts, employment and payroll for NAICS 721 (Accommodation and Food Services > Accommodation) — a free, long-run, granular US hotel-supply census (number of hotel establishments, employment) that could be turned into a US hotel-supply-growth series to compare against Airbnb's US listing growth. Directly addresses gap 8 (hotel supply) with public, county-level government data going back further than any commercial STR/CoStar series we hold.
